abstract: ABSTRACT Protein phosphorylation plays a pivotal role in cellular signal transduction and plant development. The plant steroid hormone Brassinosteroids (BRs) signal transduction relies primarily on protein kinase‐mediated phosphorylation cascades. However, the specific mechanisms of phosphorylation regulation in BR signalling remain to be fully elucidated. This study focuses on BIN2, an indispensable protein kinase in the BR signalling pathway, utilising single‐celled cotton fibre to investigate the mechanisms by which phosphorylation regulates cell elongation. Firstly, we confirmed the inhibitory role of GhBIN2 in fibre elongation through its overexpression. Subsequently, we employed 4D‐fastDIA quantitative phosphoproteomics and proteomics analysis to map the GhBIN2‐mediated phosphorylation regulatory network. Through a comprehensive analysis of this network, we identified six credible substrates of GhBIN2. Further investigation revealed that GhBIN2 interacts with substrate GhIQD14 and increases its abundance through phosphorylation to negatively regulate fibre elongation. This study deepens the understanding of BR signalling in cotton fibre elongation and provides experimental evidence and new insights for comprehending the regulatory role of protein phosphorylation in plant cell elongation processes.

Materials and Methods
4.1
Plant Material and Growth Conditions
The upland cotton genotype ZM49 (
Gossypium hirsutum
L.) was used as the recipient for genetic transformation in this study. Cotton plants were grown in a controlled environment chamber, maintained at a constant temperature of 28°C with a 16‐h light/8‐h dark cycle. During the first month post‐germination, seedlings were cultivated in a soil mix composed of 3 parts vermiculite to 1 part commercial potting soil (v/v). After this initial period, the plants were transferred to a mixture of loess and potting soil in a 1:2 ratio (v/v). A regular irrigation schedule was followed, with irrigation every 72 h to ensure adequate soil moisture.
4.2
Amplification‐Mutagenesis and Construction of Overexpression Plants
To create specific point mutations of the
GhBIN2
gene, site‐directed mutagenesis was performed using PrimerX (
http://www.bioinformatics.org/primerx/cgi‐bin/DNA_1.cgi
) to introduce point mutations at previously reported loci (Li and Nam
2002
). Genomic DNA (gDNA) was extracted from ZM49 cotton using the Tiangen DNA isolation kit, and complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesised via reverse transcription. Mutated
GhBIN2
sequences were amplified from gDNA and cDNA templates using fusion PCR. The
GhIQD14
gene fragment was also amplified from cDNA by standard PCR methods. The WMV067 vector containing the 35S promoter was double‐digested with BamHI and SalI restriction enzymes, and the
GhBIN2
and
GhIQD14
genes were then inserted into it. The recombinant plasmid was verified by sequencing and subsequently transformed into
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
strain EHA105. Positive clones were screened using colony PCR. Finally, transgenic cotton plants overexpressing the genes of interest were obtained using the shoot apical meristem cell‐mediated transformation system (SAMT) (Ge et al.
2023
).
4.3
Virus‐Induced Gene Silencing
A highly specific 300 bp fragment of the
GhBIN2
/
GhIQD14
coding sequence was cloned into the pCLCrV‐A vector. Recombinant and empty vector plasmids were individually introduced into
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
strain GV3101. When cotton seedlings developed fully expanded cotyledons, they were infiltrated with
Agrobacterium
suspensions using a syringe until saturation was achieved. Following infiltration, seedlings were incubated in darkness for 24 h and then transferred to a greenhouse maintained at 28°C under a 16‐h light/8‐h dark photoperiod for continued growth.
4.4
Construction of
Arabidopsis
Overexpression Lines
The
Arabidopsis thaliana
ecotype Columbia‐0 (Col‐0) was used as the background genotype for transformation. Plants were grown in a controlled growth chamber set at 22°C with a 16‐h light/8‐h dark cycle. The full‐length and mutated cDNA sequences of
GhIQD14
were cloned into the pCAMBIA‐2300 vector, and the resulting constructs were introduced into
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
strain GV3101. Col‐0 plants were transformed using the floral dip method. Transgenic seeds were collected and germinated on ½ Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin for selection. Positive transgenic lines were confirmed at both RNA and protein levels before being subjected to phenotypic evaluation.
4.5
Evolution and Expression Analysis of the
GhSK2s
Family Genes
The amino acid sequence of the
Arabidopsis SK21
gene was retrieved from the TAIR database (
https://www.arabidopsis.org/
), whereas sequences of cotton
GhSK2s
family members were obtained from the CottonFGD database (
https://www.elabcaas.cn/
). Multiple sequence alignments of the full‐length protein sequences were performed using MEGA7.0 software (Kumar et al.
2008
), and a phylogenetic tree was constructed using the Neighbour‐Joining method with 1000 bootstrap replications and a 95% site coverage cutoff (Qanmber, Liu, et al.
2019
; Qanmber, Lu, et al.
2019
; Qanmber, Ali, et al.
2019
). The alignments were visualised using Jalview software (
https://www.jalview.org/
). Expression patterns of
GhSK21
and
GhSK22
in different cotton tissues were analysed by examining published transcriptome sequencing data, and heatmaps were generated using TBtools software to illustrate their expression profiles (Chen, Wu, et al.
2023
).
4.6
RNA
Extraction and Quantitative Real Time
PCR
Analysis
Various cotton samples, including different organs from ZM49 plants grown in the Anyang (Hennan, China) field and 10 DPA fibres from transgenic plants and their WT controls grown in the laboratory, were rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen and ground into fine powder. Total RNA was extracted using the TianGen plant RNA extraction kit, following the manufacturer's protocol. RNA quality and quantity were assessed before reverse transcription into cDNA. Quantitative PCR was performed using TaKaRa's Premix Ex Taq II on a Roche LightCycler 480 real time PCR system, with the following amplification conditions: initial denaturation at 95°C for 10 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 10 s and annealing/extension at 60°C for 30 s.
4.7
Phenotypic Analysis of Cotton
Morphometric analysis of the cotton bolls was performed using a precision digital calliper with an accuracy of ±0.03 mm to measure longitudinal and lateral dimensions. Fibre length was quantitatively assessed using the ImageJ software (
https://imagej.nih.gov/ij/
) at 10, 15 and 20 DPA, as well as at the mature fibre stage. Each time point included 15 biological replicates for statistical accuracy. High‐resolution environmental scanning electron microscopy (ESEM) was used to analyse the ultrastructural characteristics of early fibre development in transgenic and control samples at 0 DPA.
4.8
Evaluation of Protein Phosphorylation and Abundance Using Western Blotting
Fibre samples from
Ghbin2
and WT plants at 10 DPA and 15 DPA, along with in vitro cultured ovules (14 days, with or without Bikinin treatment), were harvested and ground in liquid nitrogen. Total protein was extracted using a plant protein extraction kit (Yeasen Biotechnology) and quantified using the Bradford assay. Proteins were separated via SDS‐PAGE using a 12% polyacrylamide gel, initially run at 80 V for 30 min, followed by 120 V until the bromophenol blue dye reached the bottom. Proteins were transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes using a wet transfer system (200 mA, 60 min). Membranes were blocked with 5% (w/v) nonfat milk in TBST buffer for 1 h at room temperature, followed by three washes with TBST (10 min each). Primary antibodies (Phospho‐(Ser/Thr) Phe Antibody/anti‐GhIQD14) diluted in 2.5% BSA/TBST were incubated with the membranes overnight at 4°C. After three additional TBST washes, membranes were incubated with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Pierce, Goat anti‐Rabbit IgG (H + L), Peroxidase Conjugated) for 1 h at room temperature. Following a final set of TBST washes, protein visualisation was performed using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) substrate for 2 min, and signals were detected using a chemiluminescence imaging system. All antibodies were diluted at a ratio of 1:5000 in TBST buffer (Tris‐buffered saline containing 0.05% Tween‐20, pH 7.4). Protein phosphorylation assays were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol using the Phos‐Assay Acrylamide Kit (Vazyme).
4.9
4D
‐
FastDIA
Quantitative Phosphoproteomics and Proteomics Analysis
Fibre samples from
Ghbin2
and WT plants were collected at 10 and 15 DPA, and 4D‐FastDIA quantitative phosphoproteomics and proteomics analyses were conducted by Hangzhou Jingjie Biotechnology Co. Ltd. Total proteins were extracted from the samples and quantified using the BCA assay. After protein reduction and alkylation, digestion was carried out with mass spectrometry‐grade trypsin at 37°C for 12 h. Phosphopeptides were then enriched using affinity chromatography. The samples were analysed using an ultrahigh performance liquid chromatography–high resolution mass spectrometry (UPLC‐MS/MS) system. MaxQuant software (v1.5.2.8) was used for database searching and quantitative analysis, resulting in comprehensive phosphoproteome and proteome datasets for
Ghbin2
cotton fibres during the elongation stage. Each sample was analysed in triplicate for biological replicates.
4.10
Transcriptome Sequencing and Analysis
Total RNA was extracted from cotton fibre samples of
ZM49
and
Ghbin2
plants using the RNA extraction kit (TianGen). The extracted RNA was used to construct sequencing libraries, which were subjected to quality validation before high‐throughput sequencing on the Illumina platform. Raw sequencing data were processed using fastp for quality filtering, followed by alignment to the reference genome using hisat2. Differentially expressed genes were identified based on a significance threshold of
p
≤ 0.05 and a log
2
(fold change) ≥ 1, and selected for further analysis.
4.11
In Vitro Ovule Culture
For the ovule culture experiments, 1 DPA cotton bolls from WT and
Ghbin2
lines were collected. The bolls were surface‐sterilised by immersing them in 75% ethanol for 5 min, followed by a brief 5‐s dip in 95% ethanol. They were then rinsed five times with sterile distilled water. Ovules were aseptically excised from the sterilised bolls and transferred to a BT liquid medium for preservation. In the treatment setup, BL (1 μM) was dissolved in anhydrous ethanol, and Bikinin at various concentrations (5, 15, 25, 35 μM) was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). These solutions were added to the BT medium for ovule culture. Ovules from
Ghbin2
lines were cultured in darkness at 30°C for 8 days with Bikinin treatment, whereas both WT and
Ghbin2
ovules were cultured under the same conditions for 10 days with BL treatment.
4.12
Yeast Two‐Hybrid Experiment
The coding sequence of
GhBIN2
was cloned into the pGBKT7 vector, whereas potential interacting partners of
GhBIN2
were cloned into the pGADT7 vector. The pGBKT7‐
GhBIN2
and pGADT7‐interacting gene plasmids were co‐transformed into the yeast reporter strain Y2HGold using a co‐transformation method. Positive transformants were initially screened on SD/‐Trp/‐Leu selective medium. Clones were then transferred to SD/‐Ade/‐His/‐Leu/‐Trp quadruple dropout medium, which imposes high selective pressure, to confirm and assess the strength of protein–protein interactions.
4.13
Dual‐Luciferase Assay
The coding sequence of
GhBIN2
was inserted into the Cluc vector, whereas the coding sequences of
GhIQD14
and
GhNIPA
were inserted into the Nluc vector. The resulting fusion protein constructs (Cluc‐GhBIN2, Nluc‐GhIQD14 and Nluc‐GhNIPA) and their corresponding empty vector controls were transformed into
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
strain GV3101 (pSoup‐p19). Using an
Agrobacterium
‐mediated transient expression system, the different bacterial suspensions were co‐infiltrated into young leaves of
Nicotiana benthamiana
. Following a 24‐h dark incubation period and an additional 24 h of light exposure, luciferase activity was detected using a Tanon 5200 multifunctional chemiluminescence imaging system.
4.14
In Vitro Pull‐Down Assay
The coding sequence of
GhBIN2
was cloned into the pETX‐4T vector, and the coding sequences of
GhIQD14
and
GhNIPA
were cloned into the pET30a vector. Recombinant GST‐GhBIN2, His‐GhNIPA and His‐GhIQD14 proteins were expressed in
Escherichia coli
BL21(DE3) and purified via affinity chromatography. Purified GST‐GhBIN2 was incubated separately with His‐GhNIPA and His‐GhIQD14 at 4°C for 1 h. The reaction mixtures were then incubated with pre‐equilibrated Glutathione Sepharose 4 Fast Flow resin (YEASEN) and eluted using a buffer containing 50 mM Tris–HCl (pH 7.5) and 5 mM reduced glutathione. The eluted proteins were separated by SDS‐PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes and probed with anti‐His tag antibodies to detect His‐GhNIPA and His‐GhIQD14. The results were visualised using a Tanon 5200 Multi chemiluminescence imaging system.
4.15
In Vitro
ADP
‐Glo Kinase Assay
In vitro kinase activity assays were performed using the ADP‐Glo Kinase Assay Kit (Promega). A 25 μL reaction mixture was prepared, consisting of 2.5 μL of 10× phosphorylation buffer (200 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5; 500 mM KCl; 100 mM MgCl₂), 1 μL Ultra Pure ATP (10 mM), 5 μL GST‐GhBIN2 (0.3 mg/mL), 5 μL His‐GhNIPA (0.3 mg/mL) or GhIQD14 (0.3 mg/mL) and 11.5 μL nuclease‐free water. The reaction mixture was equilibrated at room temperature before adding 25 μL of ADP‐Glo Reagent. Following a 40‐min incubation, 50 μL of Kinase Detection Reagent was added and the mixture was incubated for an additional 60 min at room temperature. Luminescence signals were detected and analysed using a Tanon 5200 Multi chemiluminescence imaging system.
4.16
Statistical Analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 25.0 software (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). Differences among groups were assessed by one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Tukey's honestly significant difference post hoc test for multiple comparisons when significant differences were detected. Comparisons between the two groups were performed using independent‐sample
t
‐tests. Statistical significance was defined as
p
< 0.01 (**) and
p
< 0.05 (*). Unless otherwise stated, all experiments included three independent biological replicates, and data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism 8.0 software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA).

Introduction
Brassinosteroids (BRs) are endogenous plant hormones that were first discovered and isolated from rapeseed (
Brassica napus
) (Clouse and Sasse
1998
). They play crucial roles in regulating various aspects of plant growth and development, including cell elongation, lateral and primary root development, vascular differentiation, pollen tube elongation, photomorphogenesis and resistance to abiotic stresses (Planas‐Riverola et al.
2019
; Sampaothong et al.
2024
; Solonkin et al.
2024
; Serdiati et al.
2024
). BRs effectively activate the inherent potential of plants, promoting growth and development, thereby enhancing plant productivity and stress tolerance. This makes them highly promising for applications in agricultural production and ecological restoration (Yang et al.
2011
; Cherry et al.
2024
; Tharwat et al.
2024
).
At the molecular level, BRs primarily modulate plant growth and development by regulating the expression of downstream target genes through a sophisticated signal transduction cascade (Zhang et al.
2024
; Yang et al.
2023
; Liu et al.
2021
; Liu, Qanmber, et al.
2018
). Current research indicates that BRs are synthesised in the endoplasmic reticulum through a series of enzymatic reactions and subsequently transported to the plasma membrane via vesicular trafficking or other mechanisms (Nolan et al.
2020
). At the plasma membrane, BRs bind to the transmembrane receptor kinase BRI1 (BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1) (He et al.
2000
) and its homologues BRL1 and BRL3 (BRI1‐LIKE 1/3) (Kinoshita et al.
2005
). This binding leads to the recruitment of the co‐receptor SERK3/BAK1 (SOMATIC EMBRYOGENESIS RECEPTOR KINASE 3/BRI1‐ASSOCIATED RECEPTOR KINASE 1) (Gou et al.
2012
). The formation of this ligand‐receptor complex triggers autophosphorylation and transphosphorylation of the receptor kinases, thereby activating the downstream BR signal transduction cascade (Li and Nam
2002
). In the BR signal transduction cascade, phosphorylation of the BSK (BR‐SIGNALLING KINASE) (Sreeramulu et al.
2013
) family proteins and CDG1 (CONSTITUTIVE DIFFERENTIAL GROWTH 1) (Kim et al.
2011
) activates the BSU1 (BRI1 SUPPRESSOR 1) phosphatase (Kim et al.
2009
). Activated BSU1 inhibits the GSK3 (GLYCOGEN SYNTHASE KINASE 3)‐like kinase BIN2 (BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 2) through dephosphorylation, which reduces BIN's phosphorylation of downstream transcription factors BES1/BZR1 (BRI1‐EMS‐SUPPRESSOR 1/BRASSINAZOLE‐RESISTANT 1) (Youn and Kim
2015
). This process promotes dephosphorylation and nuclear localization of BES1/BZR1, enhancing their transcriptional regulatory activity. Ultimately, these core effectors synergistically modulate BR‐responsive gene expression, including the activation of BR‐induced genes and the repression of BR‐inhibited genes (Yu et al.
2011
).
The glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) family comprises highly conserved serine/threonine protein kinases in eukaryotes, playing indispensable roles as key signalling mediators in numerous biological processes (Beurel et al.
2015
). Plants exhibit a diverse array of GSK3 homologues, with research revealing 10 GSK3‐like kinases in the dicot model
Arabidopsis thaliana
(
A. thaliana
) and 9 in the monocot model
Oryza sativa
(Qi et al.
2013
). This suggests that
GSK3
genes have experienced multiple duplication events during plant evolution, leading to the diversification and specialisation of their biological functions (Qi et al.
2013
). BIN2, a key member of the
GSK3
family, has become a focal point in research on plant growth and development. It primarily regulates various physiological processes through protein phosphorylation modifications. For instance, during stomatal development, BIN2 interacts with MITOGEN‐ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASE (MAPK) cascades to promote the phosphorylation and proteasome‐dependent degradation of SPEECHLESS (SPCH) (Gudesblat et al.
2012
). BIN2 also phosphorylates transcription factors PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4) and BRASSINAZOLE‐RESISTANT 1 (BZR1), promoting their ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, thereby finely regulating hypocotyl elongation and overall plant growth (Li et al.
2017
). In response to cold, BIN2 phosphorylates the transcription factors INDUCER OF CBF EXPRESSION 1 (ICE1) and CESTA (CES), promoting their degradation and thus influencing plant cold tolerance (Chen et al.
2020
). Additionally, BIN2 stabilises various functional proteins and transcription factors through phosphorylation, including the root development regulator UPBEAT1 (UPB1) (Li et al.
2020
), abiotic stress response factors TINY and RESPONSIVE TO DESICCATION 26 (RD26) (Jiang et al.
2019
), chloroplast development regulator GOLDEN2‐LIKE 1 (GLK1) (Zhang et al.
2021
), BRASSINOSTEROID (BR) signalling negative regulators MYB‐LIKE 2 (MYBL2) and ATBS1‐INTERACTING FACTOR 2 (AIF2) (Kim et al.
2017
), and seed germination regulator ABSCISIC ACID INSENSITIVE 5 (ABI5) (Hu and Yu
2014
). Through these roles, BIN2 participates in the regulatory networks of multiple physiological processes. Moreover, BIN2 serves as a key node in the crosstalk between various hormones and environmental signal transduction pathways, such as those involving abscisic acid, auxin and light, via its protein kinase function, positioning it centrally in the plant growth regulation network (Yang et al.
2017
; Wang, Zhao, et al.
2018
). Despite significant progress in elucidating the phosphorylation‐dependent role of BIN2, most studies are still limited to studying individual genes using the model organism
Arabidopsis
. Consequently, there remains a substantial gap in understanding the broader regulatory network orchestrated by BIN2 phosphorylation and its functional conservation across diverse plant species.
Cotton fibres, uniquely elongated single cells in the plant kingdom, serve as an ideal model for investigating cellular elongation and its intrinsic regulatory mechanisms (Yang et al.
2020
; Qanmber et al.
2024
). Cotton fibre development is governed by a complex interplay of regulatory mechanisms in which phytohormones play a pivotal role, with BR, auxin, gibberellin and abscisic acid being particularly significant (Liu et al.
2023
). Transcription factors, crucial proteins in gene expression regulation, are extensively involved in the regulatory network governing cotton fibre development (Liu et al.
2023
). Concurrently, epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation and histone modifications, substantially modulate the expression patterns of genes associated with cotton fibre development (Xing et al.
2023
). Additionally, the biosynthesis and structural remodelling of the fibre cell wall represent critical stages in fibre development, involving the coordinated action of numerous functional genes (Chen, Li, et al.
2023
). Protein posttranslational modifications (PTMs) are essential for plant growth and development (Dai Vu et al.
2018
; Rumiyati et al.
2024
), with phosphorylation—a prevalent and key PTM—playing a pivotal role in numerous biological processes such as signal transduction, metabolic regulation and cell cycle progression (Kusakina and Dodd
2012
; Zarikian et al.
2024
). Nevertheless, the role and regulatory network of phosphorylation modifications during cotton fibre development remain areas requiring extensive investigation.
In this study, we employed cotton fibre, a uniquely elongated single‐cell model system, to map the
GhBIN2
‐mediated phosphorylation regulatory network at the cellular level and elucidate the mechanism of phosphorylation during cotton fibre development. Firstly, we elucidated the negative regulatory role of
GhBIN2
in cotton fibre elongation through its overexpression. Subsequently, we utilised high‐throughput 4D‐fastDIA quantitative phosphoproteomics to systematically identify GhBIN2‐mediated differentially phosphorylated proteins in upland cotton, investigating the regulatory mechanisms of phosphorylation during cotton fibre elongation. By integrating 4D‐fastDIA quantitative proteomics data, we revealed the direct impact of GhBIN2‐mediated phosphorylation on functional protein abundance and established a comprehensive phosphorylation regulatory network for cotton fibre elongation. Finally, we validated the interaction and phosphorylation between GhBIN2 and its key downstream target, GhIQD14 and confirmed the negative regulatory role of GhIQD14 in fibre elongation through genetic approaches, deepening our understanding of the GhBIN2 phosphorylation regulatory network. This study provides a comprehensive phosphorylation map of GhBIN2 in upland cotton and establishes its phosphorylation regulatory network, laying the foundation for further exploration of the molecular mechanisms of phosphorylation in regulating cell elongation and providing multi‐omics datasets for subsequent investigations.

Results
2.1
GhBIN2
, A Member of the
GSK
Family, Negatively Regulates Cotton Fibre Elongation
We identified six orthologs of
AtBIN2
(
AtSK21
) in upland cotton and designated them
GhSK21
to
GhSK26
(Wang, Yang, et al.
2018
) (Figure
S1
).
GhSK21
and
GhSK26
exhibited high homology with
AtBIN2
, and both contain a conserved STKc_GSK3 domain (Figure
S1B
). To further investigate the functionality of
GhSK2
1 and
GhSK26
, we characterised their expression profiles. Both genes are ubiquitously expressed across all tissues, with
GhSK21
showing higher expression levels than
GhSK26
(Figure
S1C
).
GhSK21
and
GhSK26
share high homology and belong to the At and Dt subgenomes of upland cotton, respectively, and their expression levels were further evaluated by qRT‐PCR with specific primers. The results were consistent with the transcriptome data, with
GhSK21
showing a higher expression in fibres compared to
GhSK26
(Figure
S2A
). Additionally, in 15 DPA fibres from cotton varieties with significantly different fibre lengths,
GhSK21
expression was lower in the long‐fibre varieties and higher in short‐fibre varieties, whereas
GhSK26
did not exhibit this expression pattern (Figure
S2B
). Based on this analysis,
GhSK21
appears to play a unique role in fibre development, leading us to rename it as
GhBIN2
for further study.
In
Arabidopsis
,
AtBIN2
produces two transcripts through alternative splicing, with both encoding proteins that have biological functions (Cheng et al.
2017
). It has also been reported that mutating the TREE sequence in the
AtBIN2
coding region can enhance its biological activity and amplify its regulatory effect (Li and Nam
2002
). To further investigate the function of
GhBIN2
, we generated transgenic cotton plants overexpressing
GhBIN2
, incorporating its genomic DNA (
Ghbin2
) with a mutated TREE sequence replaced by TRKE (Figures
S1B
and
S3
). qRT‐PCR and Western blot (WB) experiments confirmed a significant increase in
GhBIN2
expression and the presence of the
GhBIN2
‐Flag protein (Figure
1A
, Figure
S4
). Compared to control plants,
Ghbin2
plants exhibited significant reductions in the size of cotton bolls (Figure
1B–E
). During the initial stage of fibre development from −1 to 1 DPA,
Ghbin2
plants showed a reduction in the initial number of cotton fibres and a slight delay in development (Figure
1F
). Observations and measurements of fibre lengths at 10 DPA, 15 DPA and 20 DPA in
Ghbin2
and its background plant ZM49 revealed that fibre development in
Ghbin2
plants was delayed, and fibre length was significantly shortened during the rapid elongation phase (Figure
1G,I
). Statistical analysis of mature fibre length revealed that
Ghbin2
plants exhibited significantly shorter fibres compared to wild‐type (WT) plants (Figure
1H,J
). Conversely, silencing of the
GhBIN2
gene resulted in elongated fibres (Figure
S5
). These findings demonstrate that
GhBIN2
is a functional gene that negatively regulates cotton fibre elongation.

2.2
GhBIN2
Is Involved in the
BR
Signalling Pathway
To confirm that
GhBIN2
is a functional member of the GSK family and participates in the BR signalling pathway, we conducted in vitro ovule culture experiments. First, ovules of
Ghbin2
plants were cultured with varying concentrations of Bikinin, a specific inhibitor of the GSK family (Figure
S6A,B
). Compared to the control group, Bikinin treatment restored fibre elongation in
Ghbin2
plants, with the effect becoming more pronounced as the Bikinin concentration increased. The best recovery was observed at a Bikinin concentration of 25 μM, whereas higher concentrations began to inhibit fibre elongation (Figure
S6C
). Additionally, when the ovule culture of control and
Ghbin2
plants was treated with 1 μM brassinolide (BL), the control group showed a significant increase in fibre length. In contrast, the
Ghbin2
group exhibited only a slight, nonsignificant increase (Figure
S7A–C
). These results indicate that
GhBIN2
is involved in the BR signalling pathway in upland cotton as a member of the GSK family.
2.3
GhBIN2
Mediates the Phosphorylation of Various Motifs in Upland Cotton
BIN2 is a serine/threonine protein kinase that participates in various signal transduction processes by phosphorylating different substrates (Wang et al.
2012
). To investigate whether GhBIN2 also plays a role in the phosphorylation process in upland cotton and regulates fibre elongation through phosphorylation, we used serine/threonine‐specific phosphorylation antibodies to detect overall phosphorylation levels in
Ghbin2
fibres at 10 DPA and 15 DPA. The results showed a significant increase in phosphorylation levels in

3
Discussion
Protein phosphorylation, a ubiquitous posttranslational modification, is essential for cellular signal transduction and metabolic regulation (Graves and Krebs
1999
). BRs, a class of important plant hormones, primarily transmit signals through protein kinase‐mediated phosphorylation cascades (Yang et al.
2011
). Nevertheless, a comprehensive understanding of the phosphorylation‐mediated regulatory networks in BR signalling pathways remains to be fully elucidated. Cotton fibres, as extremely elongated single cells, serve as an ideal single‐cell model for investigating cellular signal transduction. This study focused on BIN2, a key protein kinase in the BR signalling pathway and utilised 4D‐fastDIA quantitative phosphoproteomics and proteomics analyses to systematically unravel the function of
GhBIN2
and its central phosphorylation regulatory network in cotton fibres. Our findings uncovered the regulatory mechanisms of phosphorylation during cotton fibre elongation and enhanced our understanding of phosphorylation cascades in BR signal transduction.
3.1
GhBIN2
Regulates Microtubule Organisation During Cotton Fibre Elongation
Microtubules, key components of the cellular cytoskeleton, play crucial roles in cell morphogenesis, intracellular transport and signal transduction (Baas and Qiang
2005
; Sjahril et al.
2024
; Yessenbayeva et al.
2024
). Their dynamic balance and function are intricately regulated by Microtubule Associated Proteins (MAPs) (Hamada
2007
), which bind to microtubules and affect their stability, orientation and processes of assembly and disassembly, thereby influencing cell growth. MAPs regulate microtubule depolymerisation and polymerisation and modulate interactions between microtubules. By interacting with MAPs, microtubules can alter their dynamics and structure to perform diverse functions (Perrin et al.
2007
). The IQD protein family, as an important class of MAPs, can modify cell morphology by influencing the arrangement of cortical microtubules (Mitra et al.
2019
). For example, in
Arabidopsis
, overexpression of
AtIQD16
alters microtubule organisation and cell shape (Wendrich et al.
2018
), whereas
AtIQD5
localises to and binds microtubules, regulating their dynamic assembly and affecting cell morphology (Liang et al.
2018
).
Cotton fibres are extremely long, unbranched single cells that develop from ovule epidermal cells (Yang et al.
2020
). During fibre cell development, microtubules influence fibre elongation and cellulose microfibril deposition in secondary cell walls by altering their organisational patterns (Graham and Haigler
2021
). Previous studies have shown that BIN2 interacts with tubulin and stabilises microtubules, thereby affecting stomatal cell shape (Liu, Yang, et al.
2018
). However, direct experimental evidence identifying specific MAPs phosphorylated by BIN2 and their role in regulating cotton fibre elongation has been lacking. By integrating phosphoproteomic and proteomic analyses, we identified GhIQD14, a protein with a conserved IQD domain (Figure
5
). Further experiments demonstrated that GhBIN2 interacts with and continuously phosphorylates GhIQD14 (Figure
6
). Proteomic analysis revealed that GhIQD14 protein abundance was significantly upregulated during the rapid elongation phase in
Ghbin2
fibres. These findings suggest that phosphorylation may regulate GhIQD14 protein accumulation by enhancing its stability or inhibiting its degradation pathway. As fibre development progresses in
Ghbin2
, the gradual accumulation of GhIQD14 protein ultimately leads to growth inhibition during the rapid elongation phase, thereby establishing a negative regulatory mechanism for fibre elongation. Although the precise molecular mechanisms underlying regulation need further investigation, increased GhIQD14 levels may influence microtubule arrangement during rapid fibre elongation, causing microtubules to align parallel to the cell elongation axis. This alignment promotes longitudinal cellulose deposition, which could inhibit fibre cell elongation. However, microtubules undergo dynamic changes during cotton fibre development, and numerous IQD homologues exist in upland cotton. Therefore, more research is needed to elucidate the dynamic regulatory mechanisms of microtubules during cotton fibre development.
Notably, recent studies have revealed that IQD proteins are also involved in calcium signalling pathways and the regulation of PIN protein polarity, both of which are critical for cell elongation and directional growth. IQDs can bind calmodulin in a calcium‐dependent manner, thereby linking microtubule dynamics to calcium signalling (Bürstenbinder, Möller, et al.
2017
). Additionally, IQDs have been implicated in the spatial distribution of PIN auxin transporters, affecting auxin gradients and thus influencing cell expansion (Bürstenbinder, Mitra, and Quegwer
2017
). These findings suggest that GhBIN2‐mediated phosphorylation of GhIQD14 may have broader regulatory effects beyond microtubule organisation, potentially integrating multiple signalling pathways to coordinate fibre cell elongation. Further research is required to dissect these complex interactions and fully understand the multifaceted roles of IQDs in cotton fibre development.
3.2
GhBIN2
's Multidimensional Regulation of Cotton Fibre Elongation
BR signalling primarily promotes cell elongation (Szekeres et al.
1996
). BIN2, a key negative regulator in the BR signalling pathway, is known for its significant dwarf phenotype in gain‐of‐function mutants, highlighting its crucial role in BR‐mediated cell elongation (Li and Nam
2002
). Research on the mechanisms by which BR regulates cell elongation has mainly focused on typical tissues, such as root tips, hypocotyls and leaves (Takatsuka et al.
2018
). This study used cotton fibre, a unique model of extremely elongated single cells, to explore the inhibitory effect of the BR signalling negative regulator GhBIN2 on cell elongation in upland cotton.
As a protein kinase, BIN2 regulates the stability and activity of target proteins through phosphorylation to exert its biological functions (Li and Nam
2002
). We investigated the regulatory mechanism of GhBIN2 on cotton fibre elongation in this specialised cell type by 4D‐fastDIA quantitative phosphoproteomics. Fibre elongation is regulated by multiple mechanisms, including cell wall elongation, cell wall synthesis, microtubule assembly, cell elongation and the synergistic effects of various hormones. Phosphoproteomics analysis in this study revealed that multiple proteins involved in these functions, such as
ACO
,
CESA
and
BZR1
(Li et al.
2021
), exhibited significant changes in phosphorylation levels in
Ghbin2
, indicating that GhBIN2 regulates fibre elongation through multiple pathways (Figures
4
and
5
).
Phosphopeptide enrichment and identification analysis of
Ghbin2
fibres revealed 20preferentially phosphorylated motifs (Figure
S8,S9
). These motifs included not only the canonical BIN2 kinase recognition site (SXXXS) but also characteristic phosphorylation motifs of other protein kinases, such as PXS/TP for ERK and RXXSP for CDK (He et al.
2002
; Morris
2001
; Joubès et al.
2000
). These findings suggested that GhBIN2 may act as a central node in the phosphorylation signalling network, regulating the activity and function of multiple downstream kinases. Further phosphoproteomic analysis demonstrated significant alterations in the phosphorylation levels and protein abundance of various kinases and phosphorylation‐related proteins in GhBIN2‐modified contexts. Collectively, these observations strongly indicated that GhBIN2 precisely regulates fibre development by modulating the phosphorylation status and expression levels of other protein kinases, thereby influencing the overall cellular phosphorylation network and establishing a complex phosphorylation cascade during fibre elongation in
Gossypium hirsutum
. Additionally, several functional proteins involved in epigenetic regulation (such as DNA methylation), posttranscriptional regulation (such as RNA splicing) and protein stability regulation (such as protein ubiquitination) showed altered abundance and phosphorylation levels in
Ghbin2
lines. This indicates that GhBIN2 may mediate protein abundance at multiple levels (DNA, RNA and proteins) to comprehensively regulate fibre elongation (Figure
8
).
3.3
Investigating the Integrated Regulation of Gene Expression (
IRGE
) Provides Insights Into Plant Development
Genes and proteins, as fundamental carriers of biological functions, have been extensively studied for their direct effects on plant development (Brenner
1988
). However, recent advances in plant biology have shown that growth and development are regulated by a sophisticated, multitiered system beyond the basic functions of these molecular units. These regulatory mechanisms include DNA‐level modification (such as DNA methylation, histone modifications and chromatin remodelling), RNA‐level regulation (such as RNA methylation, alternative splicing, capping and polyadenylation) and protein‐level osttranslational modifications (such as phosphorylation, glycosylation, ubiquitination and SUMOylation). Together, these processes are referred to as the integrated regulation of gene expression (IRGE).
Recent studies have increasingly focused on these regulatory mechanisms, elucidating their significant roles in plant growth and development. For instance, DNA methylation is crucial for maintaining genome stability, suppressing transposable elements and regulating gene expression in
Arabidopsis
(He et al.
2022
). Histone modifications, such as acetylation and methylation, regulate transcriptional activity (Shvedunova and Akhtar
2022
). In
Arabidopsis
, Histone Deacetylase 9 (HDA9) represses the expression of FLOWERING LOCUS C (
FLC
) (Zeng et al.
2020
). Similarly, in rice (
Oryza sativa
), INDETERMINATE SPIKELET 1 (IDS1) interacts with histone deacetylases and transcriptional repression complexes to modulate the transcriptional activity of downstream target genes (Cheng et al.
2018
). At the RNA level, alternative splicing enhances protein diversity, allowing plants to adapt more effectively to environmental changes (Lam et al.
2022
). Protein‐level posttranslational modifications can rapidly alter protein function, localization and stability, significantly impacting growth, development and environmental responses in rice and
Arabidopsis
(Matamoros and Becana
2021
). These multilevel regulatory mechanisms interact to form a complex regulatory network, enabling plants to precisely control their growth and development while responding swiftly to environmental changes.
In cotton, IRGE also plays a crucial role. Studies have shown that DNA methylation contributes to both abiotic stress responses and fibre elongation control in cotton (Jin et al.
2013
). Notably, m6A RNA methylation in cotton fibres directly regulates the mRNA stability of fibre elongation‐related genes, affecting fibre development (Xing et al.
2023
). Additionally, the phosphorylation and ubiquitination of certain proteins, such as GhWRKY16, GhWRKY59, GhSUS2 and GhHUB2 influence cotton growth and development (Wang et al.
2021
). However, research on these integrated regulatory networks in cotton is still limited, particularly concerning kinases and proteins directly involved in these multilayered gene expression regulatory mechanisms, which require further investigation.
In summary, this study reveals that the phosphorylation kinase GhBIN2 acts as a negative regulator of cotton fibre development by orchestrating a complex phosphorylation regulatory network. We identified multiple GhBIN2‐mediated phosphorylation substrates involved in IRGE, which together construct a multilevel regulatory network governing fibre elongation. These findings advance the understanding of the intricate regulatory mechanisms underlying cotton fibre growth and provide a foundation for future research into the dynamic interplay of signalling pathways that control plant development.

Materials and Methods
4.1
Plant Material and Growth Conditions
The upland cotton genotype ZM49 (
Gossypium hirsutum
L.) was used as the recipient for genetic transformation in this study. Cotton plants were grown in a controlled environment chamber, maintained at a constant temperature of 28°C with a 16‐h light/8‐h dark cycle. During the first month post‐germination, seedlings were cultivated in a soil mix composed of 3 parts vermiculite to 1 part commercial potting soil (v/v). After this initial period, the plants were transferred to a mixture of loess and potting soil in a 1:2 ratio (v/v). A regular irrigation schedule was followed, with irrigation every 72 h to ensure adequate soil moisture.
4.2
Amplification‐Mutagenesis and Construction of Overexpression Plants
To create specific point mutations of the
GhBIN2
gene, site‐directed mutagenesis was performed using PrimerX (
http://www.bioinformatics.org/primerx/cgi‐bin/DNA_1.cgi
) to introduce point mutations at previously reported loci (Li and Nam
2002
). Genomic DNA (gDNA) was extracted from ZM49 cotton using the Tiangen DNA isolation kit, and complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesised via reverse transcription. Mutated
GhBIN2
sequences were amplified from gDNA and cDNA templates using fusion PCR. The
GhIQD14
gene fragment was also amplified from cDNA by standard PCR methods. The WMV067 vector containing the 35S promoter was double‐digested with BamHI and SalI restriction enzymes, and the
GhBIN2
and
GhIQD14
genes were then inserted into it. The recombinant plasmid was verified by sequencing and subsequently transformed into
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
strain EHA105. Positive clones were screened using colony PCR. Finally, transgenic cotton plants overexpressing the genes of interest were obtained using the shoot apical meristem cell‐mediated transformation system (SAMT) (Ge et al.
2023
).
4.3
Virus‐Induced Gene Silencing
A highly specific 300 bp fragment of the
GhBIN2
/
GhIQD14
coding sequence was cloned into the pCLCrV‐A vector. Recombinant and empty vector plasmids were individually introduced into
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
strain GV3101. When cotton seedlings developed fully expanded cotyledons, they were infiltrated with
Agrobacterium
suspensions using a syringe until saturation was achieved. Following infiltration, seedlings were incubated in darkness for 24 h and then transferred to a greenhouse maintained at 28°C under a 16‐h light/8‐h dark photoperiod for continued growth.
4.4
Construction of
Arabidopsis
Overexpression Lines
The
Arabidopsis thaliana
ecotype Columbia‐0 (Col‐0) was used as the background genotype for transformation. Plants were grown in a controlled growth chamber set at 22°C with a 16‐h light/8‐h dark cycle. The full‐length and mutated cDNA sequences of
GhIQD14
were cloned into the pCAMBIA‐2300 vector, and the resulting constructs were introduced into
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
strain GV3101. Col‐0 plants were transformed using the floral dip method. Transgenic seeds were collected and germinated on ½ Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin for selection. Positive transgenic lines were confirmed at both RNA and protein levels before being subjected to phenotypic evaluation.

Family Genes

gene was retrieved from the TAIR database (

), whereas sequences of cotton

family members were obtained from the CottonFGD database (
https://www.elabcaas.cn/
). Multiple sequence alignments of the full‐length protein sequences were performed using MEGA7.0 software (Kumar et al.
2008
), and a phylogenetic tree was constructed using the Neighbour‐Joining method with 1000 bootstrap replications and a 95% site coverage cutoff (Qanmber, Liu, et al.
2019
; Qanmber, Lu, et al.
2019
; Qanmber, Ali, et al.
2019
). The alignments were visualised using Jalview software (
https://www.jalview.org/
). Expression patterns of
GhSK21
and
GhSK22
in different cotton tissues were analysed by examining published transcriptome sequencing data, and heatmaps were generated using TBtools software to illustrate their expression profiles (Chen, Wu, et al.
2023
).
4.6
RNA
Extraction and Quantitative Real Time
PCR
Analysis
Various cotton samples, including different organs from ZM49 plants grown in the Anyang (Hennan, China) field and 10 DPA fibres from transgenic plants and their WT controls grown in the laboratory, were rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen and ground into fine powder. Total RNA was extracted using the TianGen plant RNA extraction kit, following the manufacturer's protocol. RNA quality and quantity were assessed before reverse transcription into cDNA. Quantitative PCR was performed using TaKaRa's Premix Ex Taq II on a Roche LightCycler 480 real time PCR system, with the following amplification conditions: initial denaturation at 95°C for 10 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 10 s and annealing/extension at 60°C for 30 s.
4.7
Phenotypic Analysis of Cotton
Morphometric analysis of the cotton bolls was performed using a precision digital calliper with an accuracy of ±0.03 mm to measure longitudinal and lateral dimensions. Fibre length was quantitatively assessed using the ImageJ software (
https://imagej.nih.gov/ij/
) at 10, 15 and 20 DPA, as well as at the mature fibre stage. Each time point included 15 biological replicates for statistical accuracy. High‐resolution environmental scanning electron microscopy (ESEM) was used to analyse the ultrastructural characteristics of early fibre development in transgenic and control samples at 0 DPA.
4.8
Evaluation of Protein Phosphorylation and Abundance Using Western Blotting
Fibre samples from
Ghbin2
and WT plants at 10 DPA and 15 DPA, along with in vitro cultured ovules (14 days, with or without Bikinin treatment), were harvested and ground in liquid nitrogen. Total protein was extracted using a plant protein extraction kit (Yeasen Biotechnology) and quantified using the Bradford assay. Proteins were separated via SDS‐PAGE using a 12% polyacrylamide gel, initially run at 80 V for 30 min, followed by 120 V until the bromophenol blue dye reached the bottom. Proteins were transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes using a wet transfer system (200 mA, 60 min). Membranes were blocked with 5% (w/v) nonfat milk in TBST buffer for 1 h at room temperature, followed by three washes with TBST (10 min each). Primary antibodies (Phospho‐(Ser/Thr) Phe Antibody/anti‐GhIQD14) diluted in 2.5% BSA/TBST were incubated with the membranes overnight at 4°C. After three additional TBST washes, membranes were incubated with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Pierce, Goat anti‐Rabbit IgG (H + L), Peroxidase Conjugated) for 1 h at room temperature. Following a final set of TBST washes, protein visualisation was performed using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) substrate for 2 min, and signals were detected using a chemiluminescence imaging system. All antibodies were diluted at a ratio of 1:5000 in TBST buffer (Tris‐buffered saline containing 0.05% Tween‐20, pH 7.4). Protein phosphorylation assays were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol using the Phos‐Assay Acrylamide Kit (Vazyme).
4.9
4D
‐
FastDIA
Quantitative Phosphoproteomics and Proteomics Analysis
Fibre samples from
Ghbin2
and WT plants were collected at 10 and 15 DPA, and 4D‐FastDIA quantitative phosphoproteomics and proteomics analyses were conducted by Hangzhou Jingjie Biotechnology Co. Ltd. Total proteins were extracted from the samples and quantified using the BCA assay. After protein reduction and alkylation, digestion was carried out with mass spectrometry‐grade trypsin at 37°C for 12 h. Phosphopeptides were then enriched using affinity chromatography. The samples were analysed using an ultrahigh performance liquid chromatography–high resolution mass spectrometry (UPLC‐MS/MS) system. MaxQuant software (v1.5.2.8) was used for database searching and quantitative analysis, resulting in comprehensive phosphoproteome and proteome datasets for
Ghbin2
cotton fibres during the elongation stage. Each sample was analysed in triplicate for biological replicates.
4.10
Transcriptome Sequencing and Analysis
Total RNA was extracted from cotton fibre samples of
ZM49
and
Ghbin2
plants using the RNA extraction kit (TianGen). The extracted RNA was used to construct sequencing libraries, which were subjected to quality validation before high‐throughput sequencing on the Illumina platform. Raw sequencing data were processed using fastp for quality filtering, followed by alignment to the reference genome using hisat2. Differentially expressed genes were identified based on a significance threshold of
p
≤ 0.05 and a log
2
(fold change) ≥ 1, and selected for further analysis.
4.11
In Vitro Ovule Culture
For the ovule culture experiments, 1 DPA cotton bolls from WT and
Ghbin2
lines were collected. The bolls were surface‐sterilised by immersing them in 75% ethanol for 5 min, followed by a brief 5‐s dip in 95% ethanol. They were then rinsed five times with sterile distilled water. Ovules were aseptically excised from the sterilised bolls and transferred to a BT liquid medium for preservation. In the treatment setup, BL (1 μM) was dissolved in anhydrous ethanol, and Bikinin at various concentrations (5, 15, 25, 35 μM) was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). These solutions were added to the BT medium for ovule culture. Ovules from
Ghbin2
lines were cultured in darkness at 30°C for 8 days with Bikinin treatment, whereas both WT and
Ghbin2
ovules were cultured under the same conditions for 10 days with BL treatment.
4.12
Yeast Two‐Hybrid Experiment
The coding sequence of
GhBIN2
was cloned into the pGBKT7 vector, whereas potential interacting partners of
GhBIN2
were cloned into the pGADT7 vector. The pGBKT7‐
GhBIN2
and pGADT7‐interacting gene plasmids were co‐transformed into the yeast reporter strain Y2HGold using a co‐transformation method. Positive transformants were initially screened on SD/‐Trp/‐Leu selective medium. Clones were then transferred to SD/‐Ade/‐His/‐Leu/‐Trp quadruple dropout medium, which imposes high selective pressure, to confirm and assess the strength of protein–protein interactions.
4.13
Dual‐Luciferase Assay
The coding sequence of
GhBIN2
was inserted into the Cluc vector, whereas the coding sequences of
GhIQD14
and
GhNIPA
were inserted into the Nluc vector. The resulting fusion protein constructs (Cluc‐GhBIN2, Nluc‐GhIQD14 and Nluc‐GhNIPA) and their corresponding empty vector controls were transformed into
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
strain GV3101 (pSoup‐p19). Using an
Agrobacterium
‐mediated transient expression system, the different bacterial suspensions were co‐infiltrated into young leaves of
Nicotiana benthamiana
. Following a 24‐h dark incubation period and an additional 24 h of light exposure, luciferase activity was detected using a Tanon 5200 multifunctional chemiluminescence imaging system.
4.14
In Vitro Pull‐Down Assay
The coding sequence of
GhBIN2
was cloned into the pETX‐4T vector, and the coding sequences of
GhIQD14
and
GhNIPA
were cloned into the pET30a vector. Recombinant GST‐GhBIN2, His‐GhNIPA and His‐GhIQD14 proteins were expressed in
Escherichia coli
BL21(DE3) and purified via affinity chromatography. Purified GST‐GhBIN2 was incubated separately with His‐GhNIPA and His‐GhIQD14 at 4°C for 1 h. The reaction mixtures were then incubated with pre‐equilibrated Glutathione Sepharose 4 Fast Flow resin (YEASEN) and eluted using a buffer containing 50 mM Tris–HCl (pH 7.5) and 5 mM reduced glutathione. The eluted proteins were separated by SDS‐PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes and probed with anti‐His tag antibodies to detect His‐GhNIPA and His‐GhIQD14. The results were visualised using a Tanon 5200 Multi chemiluminescence imaging system.
4.15
In Vitro
ADP
‐Glo Kinase Assay
In vitro kinase activity assays were performed using the ADP‐Glo Kinase Assay Kit (Promega). A 25 μL reaction mixture was prepared, consisting of 2.5 μL of 10× phosphorylation buffer (200 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5; 500 mM KCl; 100 mM MgCl₂), 1 μL Ultra Pure ATP (10 mM), 5 μL GST‐GhBIN2 (0.3 mg/mL), 5 μL His‐GhNIPA (0.3 mg/mL) or GhIQD14 (0.3 mg/mL) and 11.5 μL nuclease‐free water. The reaction mixture was equilibrated at room temperature before adding 25 μL of ADP‐Glo Reagent. Following a 40‐min incubation, 50 μL of Kinase Detection Reagent was added and the mixture was incubated for an additional 60 min at room temperature. Luminescence signals were detected and analysed using a Tanon 5200 Multi chemiluminescence imaging system.
4.16
Statistical Analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 25.0 software (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). Differences among groups were assessed by one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Tukey's honestly significant difference post hoc test for multiple comparisons when significant differences were detected. Comparisons between the two groups were performed using independent‐sample
t
‐tests. Statistical significance was defined as
p
< 0.01 (**) and
p
< 0.05 (*). Unless otherwise stated, all experiments included three independent biological replicates, and data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism 8.0 software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA).
